name: Gradation

1.details: Core semantic features encoding measurable dimensions

projection.target: Positive tall relies on a contextually set standard. Six feet tall can place someone on the scale without settling whether they count as tall for a basketball player.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes scalar comparison and standards from positive-grade property ascription.

curious.title: Words for things that come in degrees
curious.summary: Words like tall, deep and quick describe something you can measure on a scale, and what counts as tall depends on what you compare it with.
curious.body:
Tall is about height, and quick is about speed. Each picks out a scale, and a person or thing sits somewhere along it.

Scales come in different shapes. Full and empty have a closed scale, while long and short have an open one. The standard matters too: tall for a child is judged against children, and perfectly clean sets an absolute standard.

Six feet tall places someone on the height scale without deciding whether that person counts as tall for a basketball player. That is a separate question, set by the context.
curious.try: Think of someone you'd call tall. Would you still call them tall if they stood on a basketball team?

teacher.summary: Gives a vocabulary for talking about scales and standards when teaching gradable adjectives.
teacher.explain: Gradation is the semantic side of gradable properties. This dictionary separates three things: the scalar property itself (tall on a height scale, quick on a speed scale), the shape of the scale (full and empty, closed; long and short, open), and the standard of comparison (tall for a child, which is class-relative, and perfectly clean, which is absolute). Positive tall relies on a contextually set standard. Six feet tall places someone on the scale without settling whether they count as tall for a basketball player. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Gradable is the usual word for adjectives that can be placed on a scale. This dictionary uses the CGEL-style distinction between scalar comparison and positive-grade property ascription.
watch_for: A learner might think tall names a fixed height, when the standard is set by context.
A learner might take six feet tall as settling whether someone counts as tall for any group.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as tall and short, full and empty, long and short. They place each on a scale, say what standard is in play, and try adding for a child or perfectly.
